summary: HotSpotters turns NASA's 26-year satellite fire record into something a fire department can use. NASA FIRMS has logged fire hotspots since November 2000, but the record mixes two generations of sensors: VIIRS reports about four times as many hotspots as MODIS for the same fires, so a simple question, "is this year unusual?", has no honest answer. We joined MODIS (2000–2012) and VIIRS (2012–2026) into one consistent record by rescaling MODIS with the VIIRS-to-MODIS ratio measured where both flew, 2012–2025. We tested it fairly: holding out each year in turn and refitting, rescaled MODIS predicts the world VIIRS total within 1.9% a year on average (worst 6.9%). On that record we built two linked web apps. HotSpotters (hotspotters.compare) maps every hotspot down to 1 km; you draw any area and get its burning calendar against what is usual there, and an AI copilot answers questions like "How was Los Angeles County in January 2025?" and ranks where to watch next. Burn Calendar (sigmachadsinspace.gay) is a globe with a page for every country through 14 November 2026: its fire calendar, whether 2026 is unusual, a 2026–27 forecast, a 14-day weather outlook, and places with regular fire and no mapped fire station. All processed data is open on Hugging Face.
details:
What it does

Fire chiefs and planners need to know where and when fire is usual, whether this year is out of the ordinary, and where to put crews next. NASA's FIRMS record has the answer for the whole Earth since November 2000, but it was built for scientists and its sensors count differently. We built one consistent record and two tools on top of it:

- HotSpotters (https://hotspotters.compare): a world map of every hotspot since November 2000 that sharpens to about 1 km as you zoom. Draw a rectangle, circle or freehand area and get its burning calendar, every month marked against what is usual there, plus its busiest month, most active year and long-term trend. An AI copilot answers plain-language questions, flies the map to the place, compares places and years, ranks counties or districts to watch in a coming month, and adds how many people live in them (US Census county estimates).

- Burn Calendar (https://sigmachadsinspace.gay): a 3D globe coloured by how much each country burns. Every one of 238 countries and territories has a page with its month-by-month fire record 2001 to 14 November 2026, its usual fire season and worst years, how 2026 so far compares with the same dates in past years, a 2026–2027 forecast checked against what 2026 actually did, a 14-day outlook that adjusts the usual odds with weather forecasts, and places with regular fire but no fire station mapped in OpenStreetMap within 15 km. New York and California have detailed views: hexagon maps, counties, the three closest fire stations by drive time on real roads, gaps where every station is more than 15 km away, and where extra crews would reach the most fire. The same copilot is built in. Any country map lets you draw a rectangle, circle or freehand area and get that area's month-by-month calendar against what is usual, its season and trend, compare up to four areas, download them as CSV, share a link, and ask the copilot about that area.

Try asking the copilot

Open https://hotspotters.compare (or the copilot button on https://sigmachadsinspace.gay) and type any of these:

- "How was Los Angeles County in January 2025?" The map flies to Los Angeles and shows the card: 1,614 hotspots, about 20 times the usual, the most active January on record.

- "Which counties in California should I watch in July 2027?" The outlook shades the watch counties on the map and ranks them, each with a small chart of its last ten Julys.

- "How many people live in the watch counties of California in August?" It brings in US Census population: about 10.8 million people in the high-watch counties.

- "Compare Jalandhar and West Bengal." It outlines both on the map in different colours, with a side-by-side table and their fire seasons overlaid.

- "Which parts of Burundi had the most fires in 2025?" An open-ended question: the AI writes and runs its own analysis and returns a ranked table.

- "What's the most dangerous place in this region?" Zoom the map somewhere first. It reads "this region" as what is on screen and ranks the districts in view.

- On Burn Calendar, draw an area on any country map and press "Ask the copilot": it answers from that area's own month-by-month record, for example "Was 2025 unusual for this area?"

The challenge: harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS

MODIS (Terra from 2000, Aqua from 2002) sees fire in 1 km pixels; VIIRS on Suomi NPP (from 2012) sees 375 m pixels and reports several times more hotspots for the same fires. One MODIS hotspot can match several VIIRS hotspots or none, so we join the two by monthly totals per place, not detection by detection.

- HotSpotters: hotspots are counted per 0.25° cell and month. Up to January 2012 the map shows MODIS (Terra + Aqua) multiplied by the VIIRS/MODIS ratio of its 5° region, measured over February 2012 to December 2025 and pulled toward the world ratio where data is thin; before July 2002, when only Terra flew, a Terra-only factor is applied too. From February 2012 it shows VIIRS detections seen by Suomi NPP, after merging the three VIIRS satellites (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) and counting a fire seen by several of them once. After Suomi NPP stopped on 2 November 2026, NOAA-20 is used.

- Burn Calendar: one exchange rate per country (and per county and hexagon in New York and California) and per calendar month, because the ratio changes with the fire season. It keeps vegetation fires only, at nominal or high confidence, and removes persistent industrial heat such as gas flares. Suomi NPP and NOAA-20 are never added together: days Suomi NPP missed (outages, and everything after 2 November 2026) are filled from NOAA-20 converted by that place's own ratio.

How we checked it

The usual check, comparing rescaled MODIS with VIIRS on the same years the ratio was fitted on, is circular. So we held out one year at a time from 2012 to 2025, refitted every ratio without it, and predicted that year.

- World totals: rescaled MODIS lands within 1.9% of VIIRS a year on average; the worst year is 2025 at 6.9%. The 2024 miss (+4.7%) comes from about 20 days of Suomi NPP outages, not the rescaling; 2025 is likely Terra's orbit drift.

- Countries: for country-years with at least 1,000 VIIRS hotspots, 82% land within 25%.

- Month by month, a seasonal ratio matters: the median country-month error is 21.8% with one ratio per 5° region and 14.2% with one ratio per country and calendar month (Burn Calendar's method).

Burn Calendar's 2026 data was rebuilt with the same method and matches the published 2025 archive to within 1–2% for most countries. Its forecast was backtested on 2018–2025 and the page says plainly where it does no better than the plain record.

Why it matters

A fire department can see in seconds whether this season is unusual for its own area, which months to staff up for, which places burn often but are far from any mapped station, and where to watch next month, all on one record that is fair to compare across 26 years.

Tools and languages

- HotSpotters: JavaScript, MapLibre GL with a CARTO basemap, Cloudflare Workers and the Cloudflare Agents SDK (Durable Objects), DeepSeek for the copilot, OpenAI Realtime for voice questions, Python and DuckDB for the data pipeline, geoBoundaries and OpenStreetMap Nominatim for places, US Census county estimates.

- Burn Calendar: TypeScript (esbuild), Three.js for the globe, MapLibre GL with OpenFreeMap, Observable Plot and d3 for charts, Python and DuckDB for data, OpenStreetMap road graphs for drive times, Open-Meteo forecasts and NASA POWER weather for the outlook, hosted on GitHub Pages, with every processed file published openly on Hugging Face.

Honest limits

- A hotspot is a satellite pixel flagged as burning, not a count of fires or of area burned.

- The MODIS ratio drifts slightly in later years, so values before 2012 may run 1–3% high.

- HotSpotters counts all thermal anomalies, so gas flares and volcanoes add to its totals in places such as the Persian Gulf; Burn Calendar filters them out, so the two sites' totals can differ there.

- Fire stations come from OpenStreetMap, which is incomplete in many countries; a gap means no station is mapped, not that none exists.

- Outlooks and forecasts estimate what is usual; they do not predict specific fires.

Use of AI

We used AI tools heavily and openly. Claude Code (Anthropic) wrote most of Burn Calendar's code, its data pipelines and validation scripts, and drafts of this text, under our direction and review; Claude also helped build HotSpotters (its commits are marked "Co-Authored-By: Claude"). At run time, the copilot's answers come from DeepSeek, and voice questions use OpenAI Realtime. Every number shown comes from NASA FIRMS data through our scripts, not from an AI model's memory, and the charts are drawn by code from that data.
